read 8 different files under your documents and then deleted, renamed away or emptied each of them, all inside 1 seconds.","why":"One program read a document and then deleted, renamed away or emptied that same document, and did it to many different files inside a minute. That is what encrypting a directory looks like from the kernel: the plaintext is read, the ciphertext is written somewhere, and the original is made to go away. Builds delete files they never read and backups read files they never delete; doing both to the same file, over and over, is the one shape they do not share. A script you wrote to reorganise photos by moving them across filesystems (a copy and then a delete of each), a batch tool rewriting images or notes in place (jpegoptim, exiftool -overwrite_original_in_place, prettier --write on a folder of markdown), or you renaming a folder of files to a new suffix by hand. mv, rsync, tar and the sync and backup clients are excluded in the kernel, and terminal editors that rename the original to `file~` on save (vim, nvim, emacs) are excluded too. It watches your document directories -- Documents, Desktop, Pictures, Videos, Music, Downloads -- and the source roots ~/Projects, ~/src and ~/code, so a sweep that reaches none of those is not seen here. Read-then-delete of the same 8 files inside one second is the literal signature of that k-way merge, and the enclosing `.lake-derivatives-<rand>` staging dir comes from `generation.rs:2546` / `generation_bundle.rs:1082`. Nothing outside the process's own generation directory was touched; no Documents/Pictures/Downloads file appears. Supporting evidence: ancestry is clean and complete — systemd user session -> shell -> `scripts/start-microservices-dev.sh --lake` -> `lake_generation_manage` (twice) -> `lake_sidecar_build`, with moat itself rating the parent/child pair 'common' (6 times today); the bundle's install receipts show a dozen `cargo build` runs in this worktree with no postinstall scripts, no network, no credential reads and no writes outside the project, which explains the 1.09 GB unowned debug binary; `/var/log/pacman.log` for 2026-09-07 shows only the morning `omarchy-moat 0.1.0-93 -> -94` upgrade, no package transaction anywhere near 14:54; and `alerts.jsonl` shows this is not a lone event but one of 143 `moat-ransom-file-churn` records, firing every ~5 s alongside `moat-exec-untrusted-home` on each freshly spawned `target/debug/*` binary — the signature of a dev loop, not of an encryptor, which would sweep new file trees rather than recreate and consume the same scratch layout. I could not read the accused binary (contents withheld at 1.05 MB staging limit, hash `14dcf273…` recorded) so I verified the mechanism from the source it was built from rather than from its bytes; the reasoning does not depend on any self-chosen name — it rests on the observed ancestry, the confinement of all destruction to the process's own freshly created temp directory, and the code path that produces exactly those filenames.
